title: Hoovies Garage's $39,000 Rolls-Royce Ghost made it 1,000 miles home on cardboard, and the second look found more wrong
dek: Tyler Hoover paid $39,000 for a 2011 Ghost with about 119,000 miles that sold new for $299,130, then drove it from Detroit to Kansas with a stuck-open thermostat.

A check-engine light, a thermostat stuck open so the V12 ran too cool and the cabin heat was weak, and it needed an extra quart of oil on the drive [1][2]. The October 28 video's title says the car is worse than he thought; what he found isn't reported in text yet [4].

Already replaced by the previous owner, part of about $30,000 spent on repairs and maintenance over two years, which the car arrives with [1].

time: About three weeks and two videos: the purchase and drive home (posted October 6, 2026) and the follow-up (October 28). The drive itself took two days with an overnight stop. No shop hours given.

costs.note: The $39,000 price is stated. Parts ($415: thermostat, coolant, oil) and other ($300: fuel for about 1,000 miles of V12 driving) are our estimates; no repair costs have been published. Labor is the channel's own and isn't counted. Whatever the October 28 video found isn't counted, because it isn't reported.

value.basis: 2011 Ghosts sold at Barrett-Jackson in 2026 for $66,000 to $84,700 (one modified car brought $93,500), mostly with far fewer miles [5]. At about 119,000 miles with an open cooling fault and an undiagnosed check-engine light, this car sits well below them; our estimate. The title is believed clean; it hasn't been reported as branded.

verdict: Not yet, and it may never be about profit. Hoover paid $39,000 for a car that comparable 2011 Ghosts with lower miles beat by $27,000 or more at auction, so there is room. But the room is thin for a 119,000-mile V12 Rolls with a cooling fault, a check-engine light and a follow-up titled "way worse than I thought." One big bill, a transmission, a suspension module, a cooling job done properly, would eat the gap. What the build shows is how far a Ghost falls: about 87% off its sticker in 15 years, and the depreciation is the bargain and the warning at once.
body:
## The buy

Tyler Hoover, who runs Hoovies Garage out of Kansas, bought a 2011 Rolls-Royce Ghost in Detroit for $39,000. The price is his: it is in the title of his October 6 video [3], and two syndicated reports on that video repeat it [1][2]. The car sold new for $299,130, so he paid about 13 cents on the dollar [1]. It had about 119,000 miles, nearly 120,000 by the end of the trip [1][2].

The seller was a Rolls-Royce collector who, according to the report, used it mainly as a winter car and didn't drive it much, and who spent about $30,000 on repairs and maintenance over two years [1]. A lot of that went into the air suspension: all four struts had already been replaced [1]. That matters, because air suspension is one of the classic ways an old Ghost turns into a money pit.

The car came well optioned. The reports list the original buyer's $7,000 chrome wheels, a $9,950 driver-assistance package, $5,600 rear climate controls and $1,100 lambswool mats, plus night vision, a panoramic roof, ventilated seats and upgraded Apple CarPlay [1][2].

## The damage

This isn't a crash car. The faults Hoover drove home with were a check-engine light and a cooling problem: the thermostat was stuck open, so the twin-turbo V12 never got up to temperature in cold weather and the cabin heat was weak [1][2]. The car also needed an extra quart of oil on the way [1].

The second video, posted October 28, is titled "My Cheap Rolls-Royce Ghost Is Way Worse Than I Thought" [4]. Its description gives nothing away, and no outlet has reported what he found, so this file doesn't guess. We'll add it when it's on the record.

## The work and the parts

So far the work is a roadside fix. Hoover tucked a piece of cardboard from a discarded air-conditioner box behind the grille to cut airflow through the radiator so the engine could warm up [1][2]. Both reports call it a stopgap: it can cause overheating if the temperature isn't watched, and the thermostat still needs a proper repair [1][2].

The trip went better than the purchase price suggests. He covered nearly 1,000 miles, mostly interstate, with an overnight stop in Pontiac, Illinois, and no major breakdown [1]. He praised the quiet V12 and the ride, and the night-vision camera still worked [1][2].

The real parts list starts now: a thermostat and coolant, whatever the check-engine light is about, and whatever the follow-up turned up. No part prices have been published. Our estimate for the thermostat job and fluids is about $415, which is small next to the purchase, but it's the unknown in the second video that decides this project.

## The money

In: $39,000, stated. Our estimates add about $415 for parts and $300 of fuel for a thousand miles in a heavy V12, for roughly $39,715. Labor is Hoover's own.

Out, if he sold: 2011 Ghosts have changed hands at Barrett-Jackson in 2026 for $66,000 (twice) and $84,700, the last with 34,000 miles; a modified one brought $93,500 [5]. Those are cleaner, lower-mileage cars sold in a room full of bidders. A 119,000-mile Ghost with a known cooling fault and a lit dashboard is a different thing, and we put it at $40,000 to $60,000 as it sits. Fix the cooling, clear the light, and it moves toward the top of that range.

## What's next

The follow-up is the hinge. If "way worse" means a sensor, the Ghost is a cheap way into a car that cost $300,000, which is the whole point of Hoovies Garage. If it means a turbo, a transmission or electronics, the economics flip quickly, because parts for this car are priced for its first owner, not its fourth. We'll update the file when the findings are reported.
